meta.blurb: The pamphlet names no author, only an Englishman. In January 1776 it reaches a country at war but mostly still loyal to its king. Thomas Paine uses plain words to ask why a small island should rule a whole continent forever.
meta.bible: Common Sense: the pamphlet, published in Philadelphia in January 1776, signed only by an Englishman. Thomas Paine: the author, born in Thetford, England, in 1737; he came to Philadelphia in 1774 with a letter from Benjamin Franklin; died in New York in 1809. Benjamin Franklin: American statesman who introduced Paine. Philadelphia: the city where the pamphlet was printed. Britain: the country ruling the thirteen colonies. America: the thirteen colonies. King George the Third: the British king. Lexington and Concord: where fighting began in April 1775. Gideon: Old Testament leader who refused a crown. Samuel: Old Testament prophet who warned the Israelites about kings. Israel: the Israelites of the Bible. William of Normandy: conqueror of England in 1066. House of Lords and House of Commons: parts of the English Parliament. Europe, France, Spain, Germany, Holland, Turkey: places Paine mentions. Continental Conference: Paine's idea for a congress with delegates from each colony. Congress: the Continental Congress, which adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. Thomas Jefferson: main author of the Declaration. George Washington: army commander who wrote that the pamphlet was changing many minds. The American Crisis: Paine's later series of papers. The pamphlet has four parts: the origin of government, monarchy, the state of American affairs, and America's ability to stand alone. Voice and tone: clear, urgent, respectful; a retelling that follows Paine's order and arguments, attributing each claim to Paine; plain words for ordinary readers.

B1B2: In January 1776, a short pamphlet went on sale in Philadelphia, and it was soon the talk of the whole city. War with Britain had already begun, but most people were still unsure what they wanted.
The pamphlet carried no name, only the words “Written by an Englishman” on its title page. Readers argued in the streets about who the bold author could be.
Thomas Paine was born in Thetford, England, in 1737, and he had worked as a corset maker and a tax officer. He sailed to Philadelphia in 1774 with a letter from Benjamin Franklin.
In 1776 most colonists still thought of themselves as loyal British subjects. They wanted fair treatment from the king, not a new country of their own.
Paine did not write for scholars or lawyers, because he wanted to reach the ordinary people of the colonies. He used plain, forceful words so that a farmer or a sailor could follow every argument.
Paine begins by warning that a long habit of accepting something can make it seem right. He asks readers only to put aside old feelings and think for themselves.
Paine begins Part One by saying that society and government are not the same thing. Society comes from our needs, he writes, while government exists because people sometimes do wrong.
Society is a blessing, Paine writes, but government, even at its best, is only a necessary evil. At its worst, he adds, it becomes an evil that nobody should have to bear.
Paine asks us to imagine a few people settling in a faraway place, with no government at all. At first they need each other so much that they live together in peace.
As the group grows, some people begin to forget their duties to each other. So the settlers meet under a tree, agree on rules, and choose a few of them to make laws for everyone.

Paine says that these representatives must be elected often, so that they never forget they are ordinary people like their neighbours. If they grow too proud, the voters can simply replace them at the next election.
Paine says that the whole purpose of government is to give people freedom and security. The best form of government, he argues, is the one that gives these most safely and at the least cost.

Paine had little respect for the English system of government, which many people proudly praised. It mixed a king, lords and elected members, he said, in a way so tangled that no one could explain it clearly.
Paine argues that the simpler a government is, the less likely it is to go wrong. A plain system is also easier to repair when something breaks down.
In the second part, Paine attacks monarchy and the rule of kings by birth. By nature, he says, all people are equal, so no one is born to rule others.

Paine turns to the Old Testament, which many colonists knew well, to argue against kings. The Israelites, he notes, lived without one for a long time, and Gideon refused the crown when they offered it.
Later, the Israelites asked for a king because they wanted to be like other nations. The prophet Samuel warned them that a king would take their sons, their daughters and their fields.
Paine asks why a king's child should rule only because of who his father was. Nature, he says, does not pass wisdom or goodness down from one person to the next.
Paine suggests that the first king was probably the leader of a gang who took power by force. Over time, he says, people forgot this and began to treat the crown as sacred.
Paine adds that rule by birth causes endless quarrels about who should be king next. In England, he says, these quarrels have started many wars and cost many lives.
Paine looks at the royal family of England and does not like what he finds. In 1066, he says, William of Normandy took the crown by force, not because the English people wanted him.
In England, Paine writes, a king has little to do except make war and hand out well-paid jobs. For this the people pay a very large sum every year, and he thinks it is poor value.
Paine ends his attack on kings with a grim claim that he repeats in the strongest words. Monarchy and rule by birth, he says, have laid the world in blood and ashes.
In the third part, Paine turns to the crisis in America and speaks with great urgency. Blood has already been shed, he says, so the time for debate is over and arms must now decide.
Britain called itself the mother country, but Paine says this is not true. Many colonists came from Germany, Holland and other lands, and many had fled from harsh treatment in England itself.
Some people said that Britain had kept the colonies safe and that they should be grateful. Paine replies that Britain did this for its own trade and power, not out of love for them.
Paine says that America would not lose its trade by becoming free. Grain will always find buyers, he writes, as long as people in Europe need to eat.
While America belongs to Britain, Paine warns, it will be dragged into every European war. It will quarrel with nations that have no reason to be its enemies.
Paine insists that the colonists have a natural right to a government of their own. They should be able to make their own laws, he says, and to choose the people who carry them out.
Paine finds something absurd in the idea of a whole continent being ruled forever by a small island. The great distance between England and America, he says, shows that heaven never intended it.
Some people said that America had grown rich and strong under British rule, so why should it change? Paine answers that a child who thrives on milk should not be fed on milk forever.
The colonists had sent humble petitions to the king, hoping that he would listen. Paine points out that the king had answered them not with kindness but with soldiers and warships.
Paine asks readers who have lost homes or loved ones whether they can simply forget and forgive. A peace made now, he warns, would only leave the old quarrel waiting to start again.

Paine believes that waiting would only make the problem worse, and that every year of delay would cost more. The colonies are united and brave at this moment, he says, and the chance may not come again.

Paine offers some hints for a new government that would serve all the colonies together. Each colony would send delegates to a great congress, and the congress would write a charter for the whole country.
Paine wants the charter to protect the freedom and property of every person. Above all, he says, it should guarantee the free practice of religion, according to each person's conscience.
Paine writes that in a free country the law itself should be king, and nobody else. He suggests a public day when the charter is proclaimed and a crown is placed upon it.
Paine believes that it is the duty of government to protect every sincere believer. He sees the many religions of America as a strength, because they give people more chances to show kindness.
The fourth part asks whether America is strong enough to stand alone. Paine answers yes, and he points to its many people, its wide land and its fighting men.
Paine notes that America owes almost nothing, while Britain carries a huge debt from many wars. He also argues that a small debt, spent on freedom, is not too heavy a price.

Paine notes that America has all the materials for shipbuilding, including timber, iron, tar and rope. He believes that the colonies could build a fleet fast enough to protect their coasts and their trade.

Paine argues that other countries will never deal fairly with America while it is only a British colony. Once it stands alone, he says, nations such as France and Spain may be willing to trade and make friends.
Paine suggests that the colonies publish a clear statement of their wrongs and send it to the courts of Europe. Such a declaration, he says, would win more respect than a quiet request for peace.

Paine says that this is the seed-time of the new union, the moment when its character is formed. A small crack now, he warns, will be like a name scratched in a young oak that grows larger with the tree.
Paine calls on all who love humanity to oppose not only tyranny but also the tyrant himself. Freedom has been driven from country to country, he writes, so America must prepare a safe home for it.
This is not the concern of one day or one year, Paine says. Children who are not yet born are part of the question, and they will feel its effects for ages.
Paine says that the blood of the slain and the voice of nature both cry out that it is time to part. In one short sentence, “’Tis time to part,” he sums up everything he has argued.
The pamphlet sold faster than almost anything printed in America before it. Estimates differ, but many historians believe that more than 100,000 copies were sold within the first year.
Within a few months, opinion had begun to change across the colonies. On the Fourth of July 1776, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, and the thirteen colonies declared themselves free.

Paine went on to write The American Crisis, and he gave the earnings from Common Sense to help the army. He died in New York in 1809, but his plain, brave words still remind us that ordinary people can question power.
C1C2: In the cold first days of 1776, a short pamphlet appeared in the bookshops of Philadelphia, and within weeks it was being read aloud in taverns and homes across the colonies. The thirteen colonies were already at war with Britain, since shots had been fired at Lexington and Concord the previous April. Yet hardly anyone had dared to say aloud what this small, plain-spoken work boldly proposed: that the colonies should stop asking for peace and become a free nation.

The title page said only that the work had been written by an Englishman, and the author's name was left off altogether. Such caution made sense, because attacking the king in print could be called treason, and treason was punished with death. Readers filled the taverns of Philadelphia with eager guesses, and some of them even named quite the wrong man.

Thomas Paine was born in Thetford, England, in 1737, the son of a corset maker, and he failed at several trades before he found his true calling. He had worked as a tax officer and as a teacher, and he had twice lost his post in the tax service. In 1774, with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin, he crossed the Atlantic and began a new life in Philadelphia.

Even after blood had been shed, most colonists still thought of themselves as loyal subjects of King George the Third, and they hoped that he would listen to their complaints. Independence seemed to many a frightening leap into the dark, a step that no respectable person would take lightly. Into this cautious mood Paine threw a pamphlet written to shake people out of their old habits of thought.

Where other writers of the time chose long, learned sentences full of Latin and legal terms, Paine chose short and forceful words that a farmer or a sailor could follow. He wanted ordinary people, and not only educated gentlemen, to feel that the whole argument belonged to them. That choice of language was as important as anything he said, for it carried his ideas into every corner of the colonies.

In his opening pages Paine admits that his ideas may not yet be popular, since a long habit of accepting a thing as normal gives it the look of being right. He does not ask his readers to agree with him at once, only to set aside their prejudices and weigh his reasons fairly. He agrees that time wins more converts than reason does, yet he insists that the question must be faced now.

The first part of the pamphlet looks at the origin of government, and Paine begins by separating two ideas that people usually mix together. Society, he argues, is created by our needs, because no one alone can supply every want, and it draws people together in friendship. Government, by contrast, exists because of human wrongdoing, and its purpose is to restrain the vices that society alone cannot prevent.

Paine's most famous sentence in this section declares that society is a blessing, while government, even in its best form, is nothing more than a necessary evil. In its worst form, he adds, it becomes an intolerable one, and our suffering is made sharper by knowing that we ourselves have supplied the means of it. Government, in his view, is meant to protect people, and it should be judged by how well it does that job.

To explain how government begins, Paine invites us to picture a small group of people settling in some distant, empty corner of the earth, far from every other nation. At first, he says, their needs would bind them together, for no one could build shelters, gather food and keep safe without the help of neighbours. Law would hardly be necessary at first, because kindness and common interest would be enough to keep the peace.

As the settlement grows, Paine says, some settlers grow careless of the duties that bind them to one another. The people then find it necessary to meet together under the shade of a tree and agree on rules that all must obey. When the settlement grows too large for everyone to meet in one place, they choose a few trusted neighbours to speak and decide for all.

To keep these representatives honest, Paine insists that elections must be held often, so that those who govern are soon returned to the common body of the people. Fear of losing the voters' trust, he reasons, will keep them from neglecting the public good in favour of their own advantage. In this way the interest of the rulers and the interest of the ruled are bound tightly together.

From his little story Paine draws a plain conclusion: the purpose of government is freedom and security, and nothing else justifies its power. Every form of government should therefore be tested by one question, which is whether it gives these two blessings with the greatest benefit and the least cost to the people. If it does not, then its great age and its grand traditions are no good reason to keep it.

Paine then turns to the English constitution, which most Britons and many colonists thought the finest system in the world. He sees in it a confusing mixture of a king, a House of Lords and a House of Commons, each supposed to check the others. In practice, he argues, the crown holds the greater power, so that a free-seeming government still rests on the will of one man.

Simplicity, Paine insists, is the mark of good sense in any machine, and a government should be no different. The simpler a thing is, the less likely it is to be disordered, and the easier it is to mend when it breaks. A tangled constitution, however admired, hides its faults behind its own complications, and people can no longer see what has gone wrong.

The second part of the pamphlet turns against monarchy and the idea that a crown can pass from parent to child. All people, Paine argues, are born equal, and nature itself draws no line between those who command and those who obey. Such a difference, he says, was invented by men, and it needs a better defence than long habit.

Because most of his readers knew the Bible well, Paine turns to the Old Testament for his evidence. He points out that the Israelites lived for generations without a king, ruled by judges, and that Gideon refused the crown when the people offered it to him. His reading of this story is that God, not any man, was meant to be the ruler of the people.

In time, the elders of Israel asked the prophet Samuel for a king, so that they might be like the nations around them. Samuel warned them that a king would take their sons for his armies, their daughters for his service and the best of their fields for himself. Paine, reading the story as a lesson, claims that God was displeased with the demand, and that the people had made a grave mistake.

Hereditary succession, Paine claims, is an even greater absurdity than the monarchy itself, since no one can say that wisdom and goodness are handed down in a family like a house or a field. A king's heir might be brave and clever, but he might just as easily be foolish, selfish or too young to understand his duties. To give such a person power over millions, merely because of the name he carries, strikes Paine as an insult to common sense.

With a touch of scorn, Paine imagines that the very first king was simply the strongest or craftiest leader of some rough band, a man who won his title by force or cunning. Later generations, he says, gave this power a respectable name and passed it down as though it were a sacred right. What began in violence, he concludes, can hardly deserve the deep awe and obedience that people now show it.

Paine also reminds his readers that the crown has often been a prize to fight over, since every death on the throne raises the question of who should come next. England's history, he says, is full of civil wars that began in just this way, with rival families struggling for the same title. Thousands of ordinary people paid with their lives for quarrels that had nothing to do with their own good.

Looking back to the beginning of the royal line, Paine finds no honourable origin there, and he says so with scorn. In 1066 William of Normandy crossed the Channel with an army, defeated the English and made himself king, and the English people were never asked whether they agreed. If such a conqueror is the founder of the line, Paine asks, why should his descendants be treated as sacred?

In England, Paine observes, a king has little real work to do beyond making war and handing out well-paid positions to his friends. For this, the people pay a vast sum each year, and the nation is often drawn into costly quarrels that no ordinary citizen wished to begin. He asks his readers whether such a bargain is wise, and he leaves them to judge it for themselves.

Paine closes his long attack on monarchy with some of the strongest and most memorable words in the whole pamphlet. Monarchy and hereditary rule, he declares, have laid the world in blood and ashes, and he calls on his readers to see this old form of government as it truly is. The colonists, he warns, should not imagine that their own king is any better or wiser than the rulers of the past.

In the third part, Paine turns from old kings to the crisis of his own day, and his tone becomes urgent. Blood has been spilled at Lexington and elsewhere, he says, and the time for debate is over, because arms must now decide the quarrel. This is no small matter, he adds, for the sun never shone on a cause of greater worth.

Britain liked to call itself the mother country of the colonies, but Paine denies that the title is truly deserved. Europe, not England, he says, is the parent of America, for the colonies had received settlers from many nations who came to escape persecution. Even those who sailed from England, he adds, were often driven away by the very government that now claimed to be their parent.

Defenders of the king pointed out that Britain had protected the colonies for years, and that gratitude was owed in return. Paine answers that Britain had acted from self-interest, defending the colonies only because their trade and land made her rich. By the same reasoning, he says, she would have defended Turkey for the sake of trade and power.

Some feared that separation would ruin American trade, but Paine answers that the whole of Europe is the colonies' market. Grain and other produce, he says, will always find buyers, as long as people in Europe have to eat. Freed from British rules, America could sell to any nation it pleased, and the profit would be its own.

Paine also warns that, as long as America depends on Britain, it will be drawn into every European war that Britain chooses to fight. The colonies would find themselves at odds with nations that had done them no harm and might otherwise have sought their friendship. Because America lies far from Europe, he argues, it has no sound reason to take part in the old rivalries of that continent.

At the heart of Paine's argument lies the claim that a government of their own is the natural right of the colonists, and that no ocean and no king can take it from them. Free people, he reasons, ought to make their own laws and choose those who carry them out, instead of waiting for permission from a distant court. To ask for less, he suggests, is to treat freedom as a favour to be granted rather than a right to be claimed.

There is something very absurd, Paine says, in the idea of a vast continent being governed forever by a small island on the far side of an ocean. The great distance that God has placed between England and America, he argues, is itself a sign that one was never meant to rule the other. Even in the heavens, he notes, no moon is larger than the planet around which it travels, so nature itself seems to agree.

Some colonists argued that America had flourished under the old connection with Britain and should not risk a change. Paine calls this a false conclusion, for he says that one might as well claim that a child who has thrived on milk must never be given meat. America, he suggests, would have grown just as well, and perhaps better, if Europe had been free to trade with her from the start.

Over many months, the colonies had sent respectful petitions to the king, in the hope that he would hear their complaints and make things right. Paine reminds his readers that these appeals had been answered with scorn, and with soldiers and warships sent across the ocean. A ruler who meets humble requests with force, he says, has already shown what kind of friend he is.

Paine speaks directly to anyone who has lost a home, a farm or a family member in the fighting, and he asks whether such a person can truly forgive. Friendship with Britain, he warns, would always be uneasy, since the old quarrels would only be waiting for another chance to break out. A union patched together out of fear and sorrow, he concludes, could never be trusted to last for long.

Some people begged for patience and for more talks with Britain, but Paine believed that waiting would only make the problem grow. The colonies were united in spirit and ready to act, he says, and a chance like this might never come again. Delay, he warns, would let courage cool and let fear and doubt spread through the colonies, until the chance was lost forever.

Paine does not claim to have a finished plan, but he offers some hints for a government that would unite all the colonies. Each colony, he suggests, would send delegates to a Continental Conference, and this body would draw up a charter for the whole nation. The president of the congress would be chosen from the colonies in turn, so that every colony would feel treated fairly.

Such a charter, Paine writes, should secure freedom and property to every person, and above all things it should protect the free exercise of religion according to the dictates of conscience. It would be a written agreement, not a matter of old custom, so that every citizen could read the rules by which he was governed. A government founded on plain words, he believes, is easier to understand and to hold to account than one resting on ancient habit.

In absolute monarchies, Paine observes, the king is the law, but in free countries the law ought to be king, and there ought to be no other. To make the point plain, he imagines a solemn day on which the charter would be proclaimed and a crown placed upon it for all to see. Afterwards, he says, the crown could be broken up and scattered among the people, to whom all power rightly belongs.

On the subject of religion, Paine holds it to be the duty of every government to protect all sincere believers, and he says that government has no other business with their faith. He does not fear the many different denominations of America, believing that such variety gives people a wider field for kindness and tolerance. Where everyone is free to believe as they wish, he suggests, neighbours can learn to respect one another.

In the final part, Paine takes up the practical question of whether America is strong enough to stand alone, and he answers it with confidence. The colonies, he says, already have a large population, a vast territory and a body of men ready to fight for their homes. He suggests that few nations in history had ever begun their independent life with so many natural advantages on their side.

On the matter of money, Paine points out that America had almost no national debt, while Britain was heavily burdened by the cost of her many wars. Any debt that the colonies might take on in the fight for freedom, he argues, would be a small price if the work were finally done. A new country, he adds, could start its independent life free of the heavy burden of old obligations and old quarrels.

Paine argues that no other part of the world produces so much of what ships require, since America is rich in timber, iron, tar and rope. Skilled shipbuilders already worked in its harbours, and he believed that a fleet could be raised with energy and a little patience. A navy of their own would protect the colonists' coasts and their trade, and it would also teach the world to respect them.

Foreign nations, Paine argues, would hardly offer help to colonies that still called themselves subjects of the British crown. As a free and independent country, however, America could speak for itself, and powers such as France and Spain might then be willing to trade with her, and perhaps to help her. This, he claims, was one more reason to declare independence at once, instead of waiting for peace talks that might never end.

Paine proposes that the colonies should publish a solemn manifesto, telling the world of the wrongs they have suffered and stating plainly that they intend to be free. This statement, he says, should be sent to the courts of Europe, where it would carry far more weight than a humble petition to a king who would not listen. Paine adds that such a statement must be honest and open, because a quiet or secret appeal would persuade no one.

Now, Paine declares, is the seed-time of continental union, faith and honour, when every action will shape the character of the new nation. He compares a fault made today to a name carved with a pin into the bark of a young oak, since the scar will widen as the tree grows. Future generations, he says, will read it in full-grown letters, so the colonies must take care to begin well.

In a famous passage, Paine calls on everyone who loves mankind to stand forth and to oppose not only the tyranny but the tyrant himself. Freedom, he says, has been hunted round the globe, and most of the old world will not give her a home. Let America, he begs, receive the fugitive and prepare in good time a refuge for all of humanity.

The issue, Paine insists, is not the concern of a single day, a year or an age, for posterity is involved in the contest and will feel its effects to the end of time. Those who will one day live in the new nation, or under the old yoke, have not yet been born and cannot speak for themselves. His readers are therefore asked to act as trustees for generations to come, and to choose as wisely and bravely as they can.

Paine's argument reaches its climax when he declares that the blood of the slain and the weeping voice of nature cry out that it is time to part. The sentence is short and blunt, but it gathers up every complaint and every grief that came before it in the pamphlet. After this, he suggests, no honest colonist could still pretend that the old bond might be mended with a few kind words.

Few pamphlets in American history sold as quickly as Common Sense, and the printers could hardly keep up with the demand. Estimates differ, but many historians believe that well over one hundred thousand copies were sold within a year, an astonishing figure for a country of about two and a half million people. Because many more people heard it read aloud in taverns and meeting places, its real audience was far larger still.

George Washington wrote early in 1776 that Common Sense was working a powerful change in the minds of many men, and across the colonies the idea of independence slowly lost its terror. On the Fourth of July 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, a document largely written by Thomas Jefferson. Historians still debate how much credit Paine's pamphlet deserves, but few doubt that it helped to prepare the ground.

Paine went on to write The American Crisis, a series of papers that encouraged the army during its darkest months, and he gave the earnings of his famous pamphlet to help buy supplies for the soldiers. He died in New York in 1809, far from the fame he had once known, and only a few people came to his funeral. Yet Common Sense remains a lasting lesson in how plain words, honestly chosen, can persuade a whole people to question power and imagine a new beginning.
